structure.title: I
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick Carraway, Nick Carraway, reflecting on his father’s advice to reserve judgment, which has made him a reluctant confidant to young men whose intimate revelations he finds overwrought and plagiaristic; after returning from the East last autumn, he sought moral order and withdrew from such confessions—except for Gatsby, whom he uniquely admired for his extraordinary gift of hope and romantic readiness, disturbed only by the 'foul dust' that followed Gatsby’s dreams, not by Gatsby himself. In the spring of 1922, Nick rents a modest eighty-dollar-a-month bungalow in West Egg, feeling initially lonely until a stranger asks him for directions to West Egg village, granting him a sense of belonging; he prepares for the bond business by purchasing twelve volumes on banking and investment securities. One evening, he drives by car to East Egg to dine with his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom, whom he knew at Yale, where they are joined by Jordan Baker, lying motionless on a couch until she suddenly speaks; during dinner, Tom delivers a racist monologue about 'The Rise of the Coloured Empires,' and a phone call from New York interrupts the meal, prompting Daisy to whisper an odd anecdote about the butler’s nose and then confess she hopes her daughter will be a 'beautiful little fool.' Afterward, Nick returns home by car, sits on an abandoned grass roller in his yard, and observes a mysterious figure—Gatsby—standing alone in the shadows of the neighboring mansion, stretching his arms toward the dark water and trembling as he gazes at a single green light far across the bay, before vanishing into the night.

structure.title: II
structure.summary: On a summer afternoon, Nick Carraway travels by train with Tom Buchanan from West Egg to New York, stopping at the desolate Valley of Ashes where Tom forcibly drags him off to George Wilson’s run-down garage; there, Myrtle Wilson emerges, ignores her husband, and asserts control over the situation, arranging to meet Tom and Nick in New York. They board separate train cars to avoid scrutiny, and upon arrival in New York, Myrtle buys a $10 Airedale puppy from a street vendor before riding with them in a lavender taxicab to her rented apartment on 158th Street. Once inside, she changes into a cream chiffon dress, calls her sister Catherine and the McKees, and hosts a rowdy gathering fueled by whisky, during which she drunkenly shouts Daisy’s name, provoking Tom to violently break her nose with his open hand; amidst bloodstained towels, scolding women, and dazed guests, Mr. McKee leaves, and Nick escapes the chaos, eventually finding himself exhausted and half-asleep in the cold waiting area of Pennsylvania Station, awaiting the four o’clock train.

structure.title: III
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick Carraway arriving by car at Jay Gatsby’s opulent Long Island mansion on a Saturday evening, where he wanders among uninvited guests amid lavish details—five crates of oranges delivered weekly, a full orchestra, and servants repairing nightly damage—while overhearing wild rumors that Gatsby killed a man or was a German spy. After failing to locate Gatsby, Nick Carraway meets Jordan Baker and encounters a drunken guest in the library who confirms Gatsby’s books are real, not props; at midnight, the party peaks with performances and champagne, yet Gatsby remains unseen until Nick Carraway, while drinking at a table, discovers the host is the man he has been conversing with, who then invites him to ride in his hydroplane the next morning. As the party descends into chaos—champagne-fueled tears, marital fights, and a car crash involving Owl Eyes and an unidentified passenger who asks for a gas station despite the detached wheel—Nick Carraway departs to find Gatsby standing alone on the porch, formally bidding farewell under the moon. Later, reflecting on midsummer in New York, Nick Carraway recounts his daily commute on foot to the Probity Trust, dinners at the Yale Club, and walks along Madison and Fifth Avenues where he fantasizes about romantic encounters, before reconnecting with Jordan Baker, whom he grows disillusioned with after learning she lied about damaging a borrowed car and cheated in a golf tournament; though drawn to her, he feels constrained by his obligation to end letters signed 'Love, Nick' to a woman back home, ultimately asserting he is one of the few honest people he has ever known.

structure.title: IV
structure.summary: On a Sunday morning, Gatsby’s mansion hosts a wild, glittering party attended by a chaotic mix of East Egg and West Egg elites, New York socialites, and theatrical figures, all drawn by his hospitality yet ignorant of his true identity; guests like Ripley Snell, who is run over after passing out on the gravel drive, and Klipspringer, who becomes a permanent 'boarder,' indulge in cocktails and roses while spreading baseless rumors—such as that Gatsby killed a man connected to Von Hindenburg—while Nick Carraway recalls over thirty named guests from a deteriorating July 5th, 1922 timetable. Later, Gatsby arrives at Nick Carraway’s door in his cream-colored car with a three-noted horn and invites him to lunch, during which he delivers an elaborate, implausible biography claiming Midwestern wealth, Oxford education, European travels, and wartime heroism, producing a Montenegrin medal and an Oxford photograph as 'proof,' before hinting at a request tied to Jordan Baker. At noon in a cellar restaurant on Forty-second Street, Gatsby introduces Nick Carraway to Meyer Wolfsheim, a grotesque figure with hair growing from his nostrils and cuff buttons made of human molars, who recounts the murder of Rosy Rosenthal and later reveals he fixed the 1919 World Series, shocking Nick Carraway; Gatsby abruptly leaves to make a phone call and vanishes before being introduced to Tom Buchanan. In a flashback, Jordan Baker recalls encountering Daisy Fay in a white roadster with Lieutenant Jay Gatsby in Louisville in October 1917, admiring his gaze, and later witnessing Daisy’s turbulent engagement and marriage to Tom Buchanan in June 1919, including her drunken breakdown on the wedding morning as she clutched the $350,000 pearl necklace before being calmed with ammonia and ice. After leaving the Plaza, Jordan reveals to Nick Carraway that Gatsby bought his mansion solely so Daisy could see the green light across the bay and asks him to invite Daisy over for tea so Gatsby can visit unseen, fearing to offend by asking Jordan directly, prompting Nick Carraway to shift focus from Gatsby’s obsession to his own growing closeness with Jordan as twilight falls.

structure.title: V
structure.summary: On a late night in West Egg, Nick returns home to find Gatsby’s mansion brilliantly lit with no party in progress, and Gatsby impulsively invites him to Coney Island or a swim, which Nick declines. The next day, Nick agrees to arrange a tea with Daisy, prompting Gatsby to nervously inquire about Nick’s income and offer a vague side business opportunity—both of which Nick refuses. On the rainy afternoon of the meeting, Gatsby has Nick’s lawn cut and delivers an entire greenhouse of flowers; when Daisy arrives by large open car with chauffeur Ferdie, Gatsby appears pale and trembling, nearly knocking over a mantelpiece clock in his distress. After an awkward silence, Daisy wipes her tears and Gatsby radiates joy, inviting them to tour his mansion, where he proudly claims he earned the house through three years of labor, though he initially cites inheritance and later vaguely references lost wealth from a war panic. Inside, they pass gardens fragrant with jonquils and hawthorn, encounter Mr. Klipspringer exercising in pajamas, and Gatsby displays dozens of luxurious shirts sent from England, causing Daisy to collapse in tears. As the rain resumes, Gatsby points out the green light at Daisy’s dock, now diminished in meaning, and shows her photographs of Dan Cody and his younger self in yachting attire; Klipspringer plays piano poorly in sportswear as thunder rolls, and Nick departs into the rain, no longer acknowledged by Gatsby, who is now emotionally absorbed with Daisy.

structure.title: VI
structure.summary: A young New York reporter arrives at Gatsby’s mansion one morning, misled by rumors that Gatsby lives in a moving boat disguised as a house or operates an underground pipeline to Canada, prompting the narrative to recount Gatsby’s origins as James Gatz of North Dakota, who at seventeen rowed out to Dan Cody’s yacht anchored off Lake Superior, adopted the name Jay Gatsby, and spent five years serving Cody across three continents, learning restraint and shaping his idealized self-image; after Cody’s death, Ella Kaye inherited his fortune and denied Gatsby his $25,000 legacy, but he emerged with a fully constructed identity. Later, after a weeks-long absence, Nick Carraway visits Gatsby’s mansion on a Sunday afternoon and is startled when Tom Buchanan, Mr. Sloane, and a woman in a brown riding-habit arrive unexpectedly on horseback; Gatsby nervously offers drinks and invites them to supper, but they respond with cold, dismissive politeness, refusing to stay. That evening, Tom and Daisy attend one of Gatsby’s parties, where Daisy is both fascinated and appalled by the chaotic energy of West Egg, dances with Gatsby, then withdraws into quiet dissatisfaction as the night descends into drunken absurdity; Gatsby, desperate for Daisy to declare she never loved Tom and reclaim their lost past, clings to the delusion that he can repeat the past, recalling the moonlit night five years earlier when he first kissed her and believed he could transcend time.

structure.title: VII
structure.summary: On a broiling summer afternoon, Nick Carraway arrives by train at the Buchanans’ house, where he finds Gatsby waiting nervously; Daisy kisses Gatsby and declares her love in front of Tom, who reacts with stunned disbelief, prompting Tom to insist they all drive to town. During the journey, they stop at Wilson’s garage under the faded eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg, where Tom coldly offers to sell Wilson his old car while Wilson, visibly ill and shaken, reveals his plan to flee with Myrtle. The group then travels to the Plaza Hotel in New York, where a volatile confrontation erupts: Tom aggressively challenges Gatsby’s claim to have attended Oxford and exposes his bootlegging ties to Meyer Wolfsheim; Daisy, under pressure, admits she once loved Tom, shattering Gatsby’s idealized vision. Afterward, Daisy and Gatsby leave in Gatsby’s blue coupé, while Tom, Nick, and Jordan drive back toward Long Island. Later that evening, Myrtle Wilson is struck and killed by a speeding car—later identified as yellow—while running into the road from Wilson’s garage; Michaelis witnesses the crash and initially describes the car as light green. Tom and Nick arrive at the scene to find Myrtle’s body under a swinging yellow light and Wilson in hysterics, crying 'Oh, my Ga-od!'; Tom insists the yellow car was not his and is corroborated by alibis, but is visibly shaken. That night, Nick waits outside the Buchanan house and finds Gatsby standing vigil in the moonlight, having spent the entire night guarding Daisy from Tom’s rage, believing she was driving the fatal car; through the pantry window, Nick sees Tom and Daisy sitting together at the kitchen table in silent, intimate communion, revealing their reconciliation—while Gatsby remains unaware his devotion is directed toward a mirage.

structure.title: VIII
structure.summary: At dawn on Long Island, Nick Carraway rushes to Gatsby’s mansion after hearing a taxi arrive, finding Gatsby defeated after waiting all night for Daisy, who briefly appeared at her window before turning off the light. They wander through the dusty, opulent rooms of the house, smoking on the French windows as Gatsby reveals his past: how he fell for Daisy as a penniless officer, falsely presented himself as wealthy, and became irrevocably bound to her dream, even after being mistakenly sent to Oxford while she chose Tom Buchanan amid her emotional turmoil. Gatsby clings to the belief that Daisy never loved Tom and insists on waiting for her, refusing Nick Carraway’s plea to flee to Atlantic City or Montreal. Later, after breakfast, he refuses to drain the pool despite autumn’s approach, revealing he never used it all summer; Nick Carraway, moved, declares Gatsby worth more than 'the whole damn bunch put together,' receiving only a radiant smile in return. Meanwhile, George Wilson, consumed by grief and delusion after Myrtle’s death, travels on foot from his garage to Port Roosevelt, then Gad’s Hill, where he buys food and appears increasingly erratic, eventually arriving in West Egg by mid-afternoon and learning Gatsby’s name. At two p.m., Gatsby puts on his bathing suit, instructs the butler to forward any call to him at the pool, retrieves a pneumatic mattress from the garage with the chauffeur’s help, and forbids moving the damaged open car; he carries it alone toward the pool, disappearing among yellowing trees. The butler waits until four a.m. for a call that never comes, while the chauffeur hears distant shots but does not react. Nick Carraway, returning from the city after failed attempts to reach Gatsby’s line (blocked by a long-distance call from Detroit), arrives to find Gatsby’s lifeless body floating on the mattress in the pool, disturbed only by wind and falling leaves; moments later, the gardener discovers Wilson’s body in the grass.

structure.title: IX
structure.summary: Following Gatsby’s death, his mansion is overrun by police, photographers, and curious onlookers, while sensationalist media labels Wilson a 'madman' and Catherine denies any connection between Myrtle and Gatsby. Nick Carraway, isolated and burdened, makes desperate but futile attempts to contact Daisy and Meyer Wolfsheim, interrupted only by a mistaken long-distance call that he must correct with the news of Gatsby’s death. On the third day, Gatsby’s father, Henry C. Gatz, arrives by train from Minnesota in a cheap ulster, overcome with grief yet later filled with awed pride upon seeing his son’s mansion and a childhood book bearing Gatsby’s meticulously handwritten self-improvement schedule; despite Nick Carraway’s efforts, nearly all of Gatsby’s acquaintances refuse to attend the funeral — Klipspringer calls only for his tennis shoes, and Wolfsheim declines on principle, citing a personal rule against involvement after death. At five o’clock in a thick drizzle, a small procession — motor hearse, limousine carrying Gatz, Nick Carraway, and the Lutheran minister, followed by a station wagon with servants and the West Egg postman — arrives at the cemetery, where the mysterious owl-eyed man, unknown to Nick Carraway, appears suddenly through the mud to pay his respects, murmuring 'Amen to that' when someone quotes 'Blessed are the dead that the rain falls on,' and later calls Gatsby 'the poor son-of-a-bitch.' Nick Carraway, reflecting on his Midwestern roots during a train ride back from Chicago’s Union Station, concludes that he, Tom, Gatsby, Daisy, and Jordan were all Westerners fundamentally unfit for the East, haunted by its moral decay, epitomized by a surreal vision of West Egg with a drunken woman on a stretcher ignored by passersby. Before leaving, he meets Jordan Baker, who lies silent in a golfing outfit, reveals she is engaged to another man, and they part after an honest acknowledgment of their broken relationship and his inability to lie to himself about honor. Later, he encounters Tom Buchanan on Fifth Avenue, who admits he told Wilson that Gatsby owned the car that killed Myrtle, justifying it as necessary while claiming emotional distress over abandoning his flat; Nick Carraway feels only disillusionment, shakes Tom’s hand reluctantly, and watches him enter a jewelry store to buy a pearl necklace or cuff buttons. Finally, alone at night, Nick Carraway walks to Gatsby’s empty house, erases an obscene word scrawled on the white steps with his shoe, and wanders to the beach, reflecting on the island’s original wilderness, Gatsby’s futile pursuit of the green light, and the human condition of striving against a current that bears us back ceaselessly into history.

plot_summary.plot_summary:
Nick Carraway, a young Midwesterner seeking moral clarity, moves to West Egg in the spring of 1922 and rents a modest home next to the extravagant mansion of the enigmatic Jay Gatsby. Through his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom—wealthy, arrogant East Egg elites—he is introduced to the glittering yet hollow world of Long Island’s elite. He soon becomes entangled in Gatsby’s obsessive quest to rekindle a lost romance with Daisy, whom Gatsby met five years earlier as a young officer before she married Tom. Gatsby, who has amassed his fortune through dubious means and reinvented himself from James Gatz of North Dakota, bought his mansion solely so Daisy could see the green light at the end of her dock. Nick, initially drawn to Gatsby’s idealism and unique capacity for hope, becomes the reluctant intermediary in their reunion, arranging a tense tea that reignites their connection and reawakens Gatsby’s delusion that he can erase time and reclaim the past.

As Gatsby and Daisy rekindle their affair, tensions escalate between Gatsby and Tom, culminating in a volatile confrontation at the Plaza Hotel in New York. Tom exposes Gatsby’s criminal ties to Meyer Wolfsheim and undermines his claims of privilege, forcing Daisy to admit she once loved Tom—a confession that shatters Gatsby’s dream. That same afternoon, Myrtle Wilson, Tom’s mistress, is killed by a speeding yellow car driven by Daisy, though Gatsby takes responsibility to protect her. George Wilson, Myrtle’s grief-stricken husband, misled by Tom into believing Gatsby was both Myrtle’s lover and her killer, hunts down Gatsby at his mansion. Meanwhile, Nick watches helplessly as Daisy and Tom retreat into their wealth and indifference, reuniting in silent complicity after the tragedy, leaving Gatsby vulnerable and alone.

In the aftermath, Gatsby is shot and killed by Wilson in his pool, a victim of his own idealism and the moral decay around him. Nick struggles to organize a funeral, only to find that Gatsby’s so-called friends—those who feasted at his parties and spread rumors about him—abandon him entirely. Only Gatsby’s father, Henry C. Gatz, arrives, proud of his son’s self-made legacy revealed in a childhood book filled with self-improvement goals. As Nick reflects on the emptiness of the East, he realizes that Gatsby’s tragedy was not merely personal but symbolic: a man who believed in the green light of the future, only to be crushed by a world that had no place for such dreams. With disillusioned resolve, Nick returns to the Midwest, having witnessed the hollowness of wealth and the cost of clinging to illusions, leaving behind a landscape where moral order has been replaced by careless privilege and silent complicity.
